pointers.sentence: The helpers in `django/utils/http.py`

The module `django/utils/http.py` holds `url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme`, the check to make on a URL that came from a client before it is used, and the small functions that read and write HTTP's own notations: dates (`http_date`, `parse_http_date`), entity tags (`quote_etag`, `parse_etags`), a header's parameters (`parse_header_parameters`, `content_disposition_header`) and query strings (`urlencode`).

That syntax is fiddly in ways that matter: a date has three legal spellings, a file name in a header has two encodings, and a URL that looks like a path can take a browser to another site (`django/utils/http.py`).
An empty URL it always refuses (`django/utils/http.py:url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme`).
The host is compared exactly, capitals, port and credentials included (`django/utils/http.py:_url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme`).

The limit on length protects the server from a denial of service: the parser does not validate its input, and Unicode normalization is very slow on Windows (`django/utils/http.py:url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme`, `django/utils/http.py:_url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme`).

The function came in the security releases 1.4.3 and 1.3.5, as is_safe_url, for use "whenever user-supplied redirect targets are accepted", and Django's own views that accepted one, mostly the authentication system's, were changed to call it (`docs/releases/1.4.3.txt`).

Django 3.0 gave it its present name "to avoid possible confusion as to effective scope": a URL with an allowed host and scheme is not on that account safe, and may still be quoted wrongly, as the function's docstring still warns (`docs/releases/3.0.txt`).

`is_same_domain` matches a host name against a pattern, by the rule that `ALLOWED_HOSTS` follows for a leading dot ([Headers, host and scheme](headers.md#the-host)), and the CSRF middleware uses it to match the host of an `"Origin"` or a `"Referer"` header against the hosts it trusts (`django/utils/http.py:escape_leading_slashes`, `django/utils/http.py:is_same_domain`).

`http_date` goes from the number to the text, and `parse_http_date` back (`django/utils/http.py:http_date`, `django/utils/http.py:parse_http_date`).
`http_date` goes from the number to the text, and `parse_http_date` back (`django/utils/http.py:http_date`, `django/utils/http.py:parse_http_date`).

`parse_http_date_safe` is for a header that may be malformed: it returns `None` where the other raises `ValueError`, and its callers treat a date they cannot read as no date (`django/utils/http.py:parse_http_date_safe`).

`quote_etag` adds the quotes to a bare string and leaves a well-formed tag alone; `parse_etags` splits a header into the tags it holds and silently drops any that are not well formed (`django/utils/http.py:quote_etag`, `django/utils/http.py:parse_etags`).

The code that compares a request's dates and tags with a response's is in [Cache headers and conditional requests: `django/utils/cache.py`](../services/http-caching.md).

`parse_header_parameters` also refuses a value longer than `MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`, 10,000 characters, with `ValueError`, and that refusal is what makes a request with an oversized Content-Type fail as it is made ([Making the request: `WSGIRequest` and `ASGIRequest`](request.md#the-content-type-and-the-encoding)) (`django/utils/http.py:parse_header_parameters`).

`content_disposition_header` quotes a file name only when every character is printable ASCII or a tab, the characters a quoted string may hold, and writes any other name as UTF-8, percent-encoded; with no file name it writes the word `"attachment"` alone for an attachment (`django/utils/http.py:content_disposition_header`).
`QueryDict.urlencode` is a different function with the same job for one type ([`QueryDict`](querydict.md#parsing-and-decoding)) (`django/utils/http.py:urlencode`).
The base 36 reader refuses more than thirteen digits, enough for any 64-bit number, so that a longer string cannot use up the server's resources (`django/utils/http.py:base36_to_int`).
